trial_name: ACTiVE — Automated Closed-Loop Ventilation vs Protocolized Conventional Ventilation (2025)
citation: Sinnige JS, Buiteman-Kruizinga LA, Horn J, Paulus F, Schultz MJ, Serpa Neto A, et al; ACTiVE Investigators and the Protective Ventilation Network. Effect of Automated Closed-Loop Ventilation vs Protocolized Conventional Ventilation on Ventilator-Free Days in Critically Ill Adults: A Randomized Clinical Trial. JAMA. Published online December 8, 2025.
one_liner: In protocolized ICUs, automated closed-loop ventilation improved early physiologic quality metrics but did not increase ventilator-free days or reduce mortality compared to protocolized conventional ventilation.

pico.population: Critically ill adults receiving invasive ventilation, expected to remain ventilated for ≥24 hours
pico.intervention: Automated closed-loop ventilation (INTELLiVENT-ASV) with automated titration of ventilation and oxygenation targets using end-tidal CO2 and SpO2
pico.comparison: Protocolized conventional ventilation using standard modes with predefined lung-protective and oxygenation/ventilation targets

background.existing_knowledge: Invasive mechanical ventilation requires continuous titration of tidal volume, pressure, and oxygenation targets to prevent ventilator-associated lung injury. Prior studies of closed-loop systems focused on process measures (time in target ranges, number of manual setting changes) and were not definitive for patient-centred outcomes in heterogeneous ICU populations.
background.knowledge_gap: Whether automated closed-loop ventilation improves patient-centred outcomes compared to protocolized conventional ventilation in a broad ICU population was unknown.
background.hypothesis: Early, automated, closed-loop ventilation (INTELLiVENT-ASV) increases ventilator-free days at day 28 compared with protocolized conventional ventilation, and improves ventilation quality (time within predefined physiologic zones).

methods.design: Multicentre, international, investigator-initiated, randomised, open-label, superiority trial
methods.setting: 7 ICUs in the Netherlands and Switzerland

inclusion: Critically ill adults receiving invasive ventilation
Expected to remain invasively ventilated for at least 24 hours
exclusion: Situations where the study mode could not be applied safely or reliably (e.g., practical/device constraints, inability to obtain/maintain consent)

methods.intervention: Automated closed-loop ventilation using INTELLiVENT-ASV on a single ventilator platform, with automated titration of ventilation and oxygenation targets using end-tidal CO2 and SpO2. Implemented immediately after randomisation and used throughout invasive ventilation during the ICU course.
methods.comparison: Protocolised conventional ventilation using standard ventilator modes with predefined targets for lung-protective ventilation and oxygenation/ventilation goals. Co-interventions (sedation/analgesia and weaning approach) were protocolised and intended to be similar between groups.
methods.sample_size_power: 1200 patients required to detect an increase in mean ventilator-free days at day 28 of 1.5 days (from 20.0 to 21.5) assuming SD 9.0, with 80% power at 5% significance level.
secondary_outcomes: Duration of invasive ventilation among survivors
Ventilation quality (ordered zones; first 6 h; subset)
Time in critical ventilation zone (first 6 h; subset)

headline_bullets: No improvement in ventilator-free days at day 28 with closed-loop ventilation (OR 0.91; 95% CI 0.77 to 1.06; P=0.23).
Mortality was similar at 28 days (37.2% vs 36.5%; HR 1.04; P=0.69) and 90 days (41.0% vs 40.0%; HR 1.04; P=0.66).
Closed-loop ventilation improved early ventilation quality in a subset (critical-zone time 11.6% vs 35.8%; P<0.001), but this did not translate into better patient-centred outcomes.
Signals for reduced rescue strategies and severe hypoxaemia were attenuated after multiplicity correction.

outcomes_table.note: Ordinal model; OR >1 would favour more VFDs (benefit).

outcomes_table.outcome: Duration of invasive ventilation among survivors (median [IQR], days)
Ventilation quality (ordered zones; first 6 h; subset)
outcomes_table.note: Higher odds of being in a better ventilation zone; Holm–Bonferroni corrected P<0.001.

outcomes_table.outcome: Time in critical ventilation zone (first 6 h; subset; mean [SD], %)
outcomes_table.note: Subset n=78 vs 64 from 3 centres; multiplicity not applied to zone-level CIs.
Holm–Bonferroni corrected P=0.108; components included recruitment manoeuvres, prone positioning, bronchoscopy for atelectasis.

safety: Ventilator-associated pneumonia: 2.2% vs 3.5% (AD −1.4%; 95% CI −3.3 to 0.4; P=0.13)

domains.notes: Central randomisation with centre as a stratification factor; centre included as a random effect in analyses.

Open-label design creates potential for clinician-influenced co-interventions (e.g., rescue strategies, extubation timing), although major outcomes were objective and co-interventions were protocolised.

Randomised: 1514 participants. Included in modified intention-to-treat analysis: 1201 (602 closed-loop; 599 conventional); 313 excluded post-randomisation due to withdrawal/non-obtained consent (150 vs 163). Primary outcome denominators were slightly lower due to missing data (e.g., VFDs: n=601 vs 595).

Clear separation in exposure: patient-level percentage of ventilated days on INTELLiVENT-ASV was 100.0% (IQR 80.0–100.0) in the closed-loop group vs 0.0% (0.0–0.0) in conventional ventilation. Cross-use at 1 hour: INTELLiVENT-ASV was used in 23/594 (3.9%) of patients in the conventional group.
Baseline physiology and illness severity were broadly similar between groups (e.g., height median 175 cm in both; weight median 80 kg in both; APACHE IV median 85 vs 82).

internal_validity.verdict: Moderate: robust randomisation and strong intervention–control separation support causal inference, but the open-label design and substantial post-randomisation exclusions (modified ITT) introduce plausible risks of bias and reduce interpretability for patient-centred outcomes.

domains.notes: High-income, protocol-driven ICUs in 2 European countries; findings most applicable to similar settings with established lung-protective ventilation culture. Heterogeneous ICU case-mix with relatively low ARDS frequency (2.5% vs 2.0% developing ARDS after 48 hours); applicability to ARDS-enriched cohorts remains uncertain.

Intervention is platform-specific (INTELLiVENT-ASV on a single ventilator family), limiting direct generalisability to other devices/algorithms. Potentially greater impact in settings with less protocolised ventilation or where staffing/workload constrains frequent manual titration.

external_validity.verdict: Moderate and context-dependent: generalisable to high-resource ICUs using similar ventilator platforms and protocolised care, but uncertain transfer to low-resource settings, different devices, or ARDS-dominant populations.

strengths: Large, multicentre, international RCT with early initiation of the assigned ventilation strategy.
Clear separation of the intervention exposure with minimal cross-use in the control group.
Prespecified statistical approach for a bounded, skewed primary endpoint and multiplicity control for secondary outcomes.
High follow-up completion through 90 days as reported in the manuscript.
limitations: Open-label design with clinician-mediated components (rescue therapies; extubation decisions) that could influence composites such as VFDs.
Substantial post-randomisation exclusions due to consent withdrawal/non-obtainment, resulting in a modified ITT analysis set.
Ventilation quality analysis was conducted in a subset from 3 centres, potentially limiting generalisability of mechanistic findings.
Control arm used protocolised conventional ventilation (not 'usual care'), potentially reducing detectable effect size in a high-performing system.

critical_appraisal.summary: A well-conducted, large RCT with strong intervention separation, but the open-label design and modified ITT analysis introduce bias risks that temper confidence in the neutral patient-centred findings, despite a clear mechanistic signal for improved ventilation quality.
strengths: Large sample size with early, protocolized intervention delivery.
Excellent separation of the intervention with minimal crossover.
Appropriate statistical handling of a complex primary endpoint.
weaknesses: Open-label design susceptible to performance bias for clinician-mediated outcomes.
High rate of post-randomisation exclusions (313/1514) deviates from a true ITT principle.
Key mechanistic finding derived from a small, non-random subset of centres.

sections.authors_conclusion: Automated closed-loop ventilation did not improve VFDs at day 28 and did not reduce mortality. Closed-loop ventilation improved early ventilation quality in a subset, supporting that the algorithm meaningfully altered delivered ventilation.

clinical_bottom_line.verdict: In high-performing ICUs with protocolised conventional ventilation, automation may improve process metrics without translating into more ventilator-free days. Implementation decisions should consider device availability, staffing/workload, and whether local usual care leaves meaningful room for improvement.
clinical_bottom_line.applies_to: High-resource, protocol-driven ICUs using a similar ventilator platform and lung-protective ventilation culture.
clinical_bottom_line.does_not_mean: Closed-loop ventilation is harmful or should be abandoned; it is a process optimiser whose patient-centred benefit is context-dependent.
implementation_caveats: Benefit may be greater in settings with less protocolised care or staffing constraints.
Findings are specific to the INTELLiVENT-ASV system and may not apply to other closed-loop algorithms.
The low ARDS rate limits conclusions for populations with more severe gas exchange impairment.

controversies.notes: Post-randomisation exclusions due to deferred/withdrawn consent (313/1514 randomised) shift interpretation away from a strict intention-to-treat framework and increase vulnerability to bias if exclusions are not exchangeable between groups.

Ventilator-free days are a composite with structural zeros (death) and a bounded, often skewed distribution; ACTiVE’s ordinal modelling approach aligns with modern methodological recommendations, but component outcomes (mortality and duration among survivors) remain essential for clinical interpretation.

A key 'success' signal (improved ventilation quality) was derived from a centre-limited subset, raising questions about representativeness and the extent to which early process improvements translate into patient-centred outcomes at scale.

unresolved_questions: Would closed-loop ventilation show patient-centred benefit in settings with lower baseline adherence to lung-protective ventilation?
Are there specific subphenotypes (e.g., ARDS) that derive greater benefit from automated titration?
How do different closed-loop algorithms compare in their effects on both process and patient-centred outcomes?

quick_recall.one_line_takeaway: Automated closed-loop ventilation improves physiologic metrics but does not increase ventilator-free days or survival in protocolized ICUs, making its benefit context-dependent rather than universal.
